newsitem.title: FINLAND: HOLTZMANN FITS ENSO BUT MAY BE EXPENSIVE - ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: HOLTZMANN FITS ENSO BUT MAY BE EXPENSIVE - ANALYSTS.

text.p: German paper maker E.Holtzmann would be a strategically good buy for Finnish forest industry group Enso Oy, the four billion markka price reported in Finnish media seems too high, analysts said on Friday.

Enso said on Friday it was in talks to buy Holtzmann, owned by publishing group Westdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung, after daily Helsingin Sanomat reported that the sellers wanted Enso to pay four billion markka for it.
Enso gave no details.
Looking at 1995, when Holtzmann's net sales were 937.1 million German marks or about three billion markka, analysts said the value of the company should be lower than four billion markka.
Holtzmann has not published 1996 figures.

"The time period in which this investment would pay itself back with the price now asked would be too long -- about 20 years," said said Aktia Bank analyst Paivi Palomaki, adding that 1.5 billion markka would be more reasonable.

Four billion markka is around 1.3 times Holtzmann's 1995 net sales, and that is higher than the industry average, analysts said. "Normally forest industry companies are sold at some 0.9 times sales, so this looks expensive," said Den Danske Bank analyst Niels Leth.
Enso's market capitalisation is some 13.1 billion markka or just 0.5 times 1996 net sales.
However, Leth added that Holtzmann is quite efficient, and that a premium could be accepted if Enso takes over no debt and only buys Holtzmann's assets and operations.
The reported four billion is not the only price estimate heard in the industry.
Specialist publication Euwid pulp and paper reported on April 16 that that industry rumors put the required price at just under one billion German marks or around three billion markka.

Enso says in its 1996 annual report that it aims to be among the three leading producers in its key areas, wood-containing printing papers, packaging materials and fine papers -- and analysts agreed Holtzmann would fit this aim.

The onging talks also suggest that Enso's management believes in shifting away from fine paper and more into magazine paper and newsprint, which would be a welcome tighter focus on areas where northern Europe has a competitive advantage over Asia, Leth said.
"I think it would be very clever of Enso to buy Holtzmann," he added.
Holtzmann produces newsprint and super-calendered (SC) magazine paper, and a Holtzmann spokesman said its capacity is about 600,000 tonnes per year.
An official at the German forest industry federation told Reuters that the company's capacity in newsprint was bigger, but could not give any details.

Euwid Pulp and Paper, which is published in Germany, has said Holtzmann's SC paper machine has a capacity of 210,000 tonnes per year, and the two newsprint machines have a combined capacity of 320,000 tonnes per year.
In 1995, Holtzmann posted a 40.5 million German marks profit, reversing a 93 million loss in the year before.

Enso could finance a buy of even four billion markka with its $1.24 million syndicated loan, which one analyst said it had not used a single dollar of, but investors will be wary of Enso's financial position, analysts said.
Enso's target is a 45 percent equity-to-assets ratio, but at end-1996, it stood at 42.1 percent.
"A further fall would increase risk and that could be seen in the share price," said Leth.
